There is a sense that, in the German SEO context, we are approaching the limit of the old website model. As long as the website was viewed as a surface for humans, the main focus was on visibility, structure, intent, and trust in the usual sense. But if a significant share of comparisons shifts to AI agents, the website begins to serve a different function: it represents the business for machine-based selection.

- For SEO, this matters because simple machine readability does not solve the problem. If only price, timelines, availability, and basic specifications are structurally accessible, the agent simply makes product comparison faster. That does not necessarily help the business. In some cases, it even accelerates the loss of differentiation. So, in my view, the next conversation is not about how to “feed content better,” but about which business attributes should be represented as machine-distinguishable in the first place.
- Here it is useful to distinguish between facts and trust claims. Services, constraints, catalogs, and service areas are one type of data. Qualifications, origin, authorization to act, guarantees, and liability are another. The second type fits poorly into conventional SEO logic based on text and markup. If all of this remains just paragraphs, the agent does not read trust — it reads a declaration. That means the technical and strategic conversations in SEO are beginning to converge.
- Separately, I would highlight the architectural error of two layers: a “website for humans” and a “layer for agents.” For the German B2B and services segment, this is especially risky, because any contradiction between what a human sees and what an agent receives quickly turns from an SEO issue into a liability issue. A single source of truth seems like a more mature solution here than any fashionable overlay.

In your view, where does the next level of SEO maturity in the German market lie: in better content markup, or already in designing a verifiable trust layer?
